Before you turn on any AI note taker, you need to know one thing: does your state require everyone's consent? Here's the plain-English version.

Welcome to the Lynkk channel. Quick but important: this is general information, not legal advice. Laws change and situations differ, so if you're unsure, ask a lawyer or your company's legal team.

[0:25 One-party vs all-party consent]
One-party vs all-party consent. In the US, recording laws are mostly set by each state. Most states follow one-party consent: if you're part of the conversation and you agree to record, that's generally enough. Some states, including California and Florida, generally require all-party consent, meaning everyone on the call has to agree. Federal law follows the one-party approach. [VERIFY: have counsel confirm before publishing]

[1:20 Calls across state lines]
Calls across state lines. Here's where it gets tricky. If you're in a one-party state and the person you're talking to is in an all-party state, which rule applies? It isn't always clear, and courts have disagreed. That's why most companies just follow the strictest rule: get everyone's consent.

[1:55 International calls]
International calls. Outside the US, rules can be stricter. In many countries, privacy laws cover how recordings are stored and used, not just whether you can record. If you talk to customers abroad, check with your legal team, and keep your consent habits consistent.

[2:35 How to ask for consent]
How to ask for consent. Keep it simple and early. Put a line in the calendar invite: "This call may be recorded for note-taking." Then say it at the start: "Mind if we record so we can focus on you instead of our notes?" If anyone says no, don't record. Write notes the old-fashioned way.

[3:15 How note takers tell people they're recording]
How note takers tell people. A meeting bot shows up in the participant list, so people can see it. Zoom, Teams and Meet show their own recording notices. If you use a bot-free note taker that records from your computer, nothing announces it for you, so you have to. Bot-free is not a loophole.

An AI note taker does four jobs in about a minute: capture, transcribe, work out who spoke, and summarize. Here's what happens at each step, and where errors creep in.

Four steps, one at a time, and at the end, a four-point accuracy test you can run today.

Welcome to the Lynkk channel. Knowing how these tools work makes you better at spotting their mistakes. So let's go step by step.

[0:40 Capture: bot, extension or in-room]
Step one: capture. The tool needs audio. There are three ways to get it. A bot joins the meeting as a participant. A browser extension or desktop app records from your own computer, with no bot. Or a phone or laptop records the room for in-person meetings. Errors start here: bad mics, echo and people talking over each other make everything after this step harder.

[1:20 Transcription]
Step two: transcription. Speech recognition turns audio into text. Modern models are good, but they still trip on names, acronyms, accents and numbers. "Fifteen" and "fifty" are a classic. Mixed languages are hard too. Lynkk supports 17 languages, including Hindi and Hinglish in the same call.

[1:55 Speaker labels]
Step three: speaker labels. The tool works out who said what. On a video call, each person's audio often comes through separately, which helps. In a room with one mic, the AI has to tell voices apart, which is harder. Wrong speaker labels are the main reason action items get assigned to the wrong person.

[2:35 Summaries and checking sources]
Step four: the summary. A language model reads the transcript and writes the summary: decisions, action items, key details. This is where a model can sound confident and still be wrong. The fix is grounding: tie every claim back to the transcript. In Lynkk, Ask Lynkk answers questions across your calls with the source, so you can click through and check.

[3:15 How to check accuracy yourself]
How to check accuracy yourself. Run one of your own recordings through the tool and check four things: names spelled right, numbers correct, the right person on each action item, and nothing important missing. If those four pass on your real calls, the tool's good enough for you.

Most transcription tools pick one language and stick to it. Real meetings in India don't. Here's how to get clean notes when people switch mid-sentence.

We'll cover what to test, a real demo, and at the end, the number check that saves you embarrassment.

Welcome to the Lynkk channel. Switching languages mid-sentence is called code-switching, and it breaks a lot of transcription tools. The tool decides the call is in English, hits a Hindi phrase, and either skips it or guesses badly. Names, numbers and product terms get mangled, and the summary misses the point.

[0:55 What to test before you buy]
What to test before you buy. Don't trust a demo. Use a real recording of your own team or customers, ideally a call where people switch languages a lot. Check three things: are the Hindi parts captured, not skipped? Are names and numbers right? And does the summary reflect what was actually decided?

[1:40 Demo on a Hinglish call]
Here's a demo on a real Hinglish call. [ON SCREEN: Lynkk transcript of a mixed Hindi-English call] Lynkk supports Hindi and Hinglish, even when they're mixed in the same conversation. You get the transcript, the summary, the decisions and the action items, just like an English-only call. [TEST RESULT: show real output, with permission from everyone on the call]

[2:35 Checking names and numbers]
Checking names and numbers. Even good tools need a quick review. Numbers are the big one: "pachaas" and "fifty" in the same call, lakh and crore next to dollars. Scan the action items for any number or date before you share them. Fix it once in the note and everyone gets the right version.

Script:
[0:00 Interview setup and consent]
Ten interviews in, you've got hours of recordings and no synthesis. Here's a workflow that gets you from raw calls to themes, with quotes you can trust.

We'll go from setup to synthesis, and at the end, how to share findings so stakeholders actually trust them.

Welcome to the Lynkk channel. Start before the first interview. Write down the three questions your research has to answer, and ask every participant for consent to record. Put it in the invite and confirm it on the call. You'll need those recordings later, so get the permission right.

[0:50 Capturing the call]
Capturing the call. Interviews happen on Zoom, Meet, Teams and sometimes in person. Use one tool that covers all of them, so every interview ends up in the same place. Lynkk captures with or without a bot, and records in the room. Focus on the person, not your notes. Follow-up questions are where the insight is.

[1:30 The Customer Interview summary format]
Use an interview-shaped summary. A sales summary or a generic meeting recap will bury what researchers need. Lynkk has a Customer Interview summary format with its own sections, built for research calls. [ON SCREEN: Customer Interview summary] Skim each one right after the call and add a line on what surprised you. That gut reaction is gold later.

[2:20 Asking questions across every interview]
Ask questions across every interview. This is where synthesis gets fast. On Lynkk Pro, Ask Lynkk answers across all your calls. Ask "What frustrates people most about onboarding?" or "Who mentioned switching from a competitor?" and you get answers drawn from every interview, not just the last one you remember.

[3:10 Pulling quotes with their sources]
Pull quotes with their sources. Every answer from Ask Lynkk shows its source, so you can jump to the exact moment and hear it in context. That keeps you honest: no paraphrase that drifts from what the customer really said. Copy two or three strong quotes per theme.

[3:45 Sharing findings]
Sharing findings. Keep the readout simple: the three research questions, the top themes with a short quote each, and what you recommend. Link each quote back to its interview so stakeholders can check it themselves. Research in an afternoon, not a week.
